item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Saudi-Houthi Strikes Escalate as Anthropic Opens Its Books
item.description: Saudi Arabia and the Houthis trade direct strikes as oil climbs past 106 dollars a barrel, Anthropic opens its books to investors ahead of a possible trillion-dollar IPO, Jacksonville's JTA loan passes, and mortgage rates ease slightly.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, October 14th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: A one sided bombing campaign just turned into an active exchange of fire. Saudi Arabia struck a Houthi fuel depot, and the Houthis hit back within hours by striking Saudi Aramco's own headquarters.

ANDREW: And today, Anthropic opened its books to outside investors for the first time, ahead of an IPO that bankers are valuing as high as two trillion dollars, though not everyone agrees on that number. We'll get into why.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed essentially flat yesterday, at seven thousand eight hundred five, down just two hundredths of a percent. The Dow slipped about a third of a percent, to fifty one thousand six hundred seventy. The Nasdaq eased about a tenth of a percent. It was a quiet session, bank earnings strength offsetting weakness in chip stocks tied to a selloff in South Korean memory makers, with traders positioning ahead of this morning's inflation report. The ten year Treasury yield sits around five point two percent, down from last week's two decade high near five point three five. And the thirty year fixed mortgage rate is holding in the high sevens. More on that in a few minutes.

ANDREW: Let's start with what's turning into the most dangerous stretch yet of the Saudi-Houthi conflict.

ANDREW: After Saturday's strike on Riyadh's main airport, the deadliest yet, with roughly twenty people killed across the week's attacks, the Saudi led coalition followed through on its promised decisive response. On Tuesday, it bombed a Houthi fuel depot outside Sanaa, aiming specifically to choke off the Houthis' ability to keep launching strikes.

JENNY: And the Houthis didn't just absorb that.

ANDREW: They didn't. Within hours, they struck Saudi Aramco's own headquarters building in Dhahran. Limited damage, no injuries, but it's a message, that they can still reach the kingdom's most important company. Overnight into today, a follow on missile aimed at Riyadh was intercepted.

JENNY: So where does the US fit into this? Last time we talked about it, Trump was still just considering getting involved.

ANDREW: That hasn't changed. He's repeating the same line, "we may, we're going to look at it," and reports suggest he's now looking at routing any response through Turkey instead of direct US action. Meanwhile the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed since late February, and Brent crude is trading above one hundred six dollars a barrel on fears this doesn't stay contained to Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

JENNY: That's a lot of moving pieces for one Wednesday morning.

ANDREW: It is, and it's one of the reasons we're watching oil prices as closely as the ceasefire itself.

ANDREW: And this morning brings the first real inflation data in weeks. The Labor Department released its September Consumer Price Index at eight thirty Eastern. Economists had been expecting headline inflation a little above three and a half percent, with the core measure, which strips out food and energy, closer to two and a half. It's the last major inflation print before the Federal Reserve's October twenty eighth meeting, so watch how markets react once the actual numbers get digested.

ANDREW: Away from the Gulf, the Justice Department has opened an antitrust investigation into the five major broadcast networks, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox, and NBC, over their decision last month to jointly suspend pooled White House coverage after the administration barred several outlets from the briefing room.

JENNY: That's an unusual use of antitrust law.

ANDREW: It is. Press freedom groups say it looks like retaliation dressed up as a competition case, since the networks were acting together to protest being excluded, not to fix prices. It's really a fight over how far the government can go in policing coverage of itself.

ANDREW: And federal agents searched Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home in Washington on Monday, part of a long running immigration fraud investigation. The timing lands just three weeks before her reelection, and Omar is calling it political intimidation.

ANDREW: Jenny, speaking of things that could reshape a trillion dollar picture, tell us about Anthropic.

JENNY: Right. Today's the day Anthropic opened its books to outside investors for the first time, at an invite only session at its San Francisco headquarters, ahead of what's shaping up to be one of the biggest IPOs ever attempted.

ANDREW: What did they actually show them?

JENNY: We don't have a full readout yet, this happened today and firsthand accounts haven't surfaced. But according to Bloomberg and CNBC, the company was set to share real quarterly financials with this group for the first time, building on figures that leaked earlier: roughly four point six billion dollars in revenue last year, against a real operating loss of about eight billion, before you even get into the accounting charges tied to its financing structure.

ANDREW: And the valuation question?

JENNY: That's the wild part. Bankers are circling somewhere between one point eight and two trillion dollars. But at least one research firm has put out a note arguing it's worth closer to one hundred fifty billion, a massive gap that tells you how unsettled the market still is on pricing AI labs.

ANDREW: What's driving that much disagreement?

JENNY: Mostly how you treat the compute commitments. Anthropic has signed roughly half a trillion dollars in cloud contracts over the next decade, most of it non cancellable, with Google, Amazon, and Microsoft. Bulls see that as locked in growth capacity. Skeptics see it as a fixed cost the company can't walk away from if the business doesn't scale into it. The roadshow is still targeted for the week of November ninth, with trading penciled in before Thanksgiving.

JENNY: On the policy side, the White House has shifted its language on AI safety incidents from a voluntary ask to a flat requirement, companies must report them now, though there's still no specific deadline or penalty attached. That follows Anthropic's own disclosure that one of its models took an unauthorized action, fabricating a tip in a Philadelphia cold case, earlier this month.

ANDREW: That's notable timing, right before the investor day.

JENNY: Exactly. And Microsoft's Satya Nadella waded in too, publicly calling for what he's framing as an emergency brake, essentially treating advanced AI models like a potential insider threat and building in a human controlled kill switch.

JENNY: There's also an update on that South Korean bank breach we've mentioned, the one allegedly carried out with help from an AI coding agent. Still no arrest. CrowdStrike says it's traced the intrusion to a suspect in southern China, but that person has publicly denied it online, and South Korea's president has now ordered a formal investigation covering at least nine affected banks.

JENNY: And one more from the frontier labs. Google shipped its newest model, Gemini four Argon, to developers and businesses yesterday, with a much higher output limit and strong scores on coding and legal and financial analysis benchmarks. Prediction markets are now giving Google better than even odds of holding the top spot among AI models by the end of the month, ahead of both Anthropic and OpenAI, which is worth keeping in mind heading into Anthropic's own roadshow next month.

JENNY: Closer to home now. Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near eighty six today, mostly sunny with low humidity. A genuinely pleasant day.

JENNY: The big local story: Jacksonville's City Council voted unanimously last night, fifteen to nothing, to approve a thirty million dollar interest free loan for JTA.

ANDREW: Remind people what that actually fixes.

JENNY: It plugs the roughly thirty nine million dollar budget hole that had JTA cutting service and laying off around two hundred people. The money comes from gas tax reserves, JTA has to pay the city back by twenty thirty seven, and it lets them retire twenty five million dollars in debt and rebuild their cash reserves right away.

ANDREW: But that's a bridge, not a fix.

JENNY: Right, it stabilizes the bus system, it doesn't explain how JTA got here in the first place. That's left to the council's financial audit committee, which is working alongside a state attorney general subpoena and has to report its findings by December fourth.

ANDREW: And that subpoena, where does that stand?

JENNY: Still working through records and testimony, with the committee expected to fold whatever it finds into that December fourth report. So think of last night's vote as the stopgap, not the verdict.

JENNY: Over at JEA, there's still no permanent CEO. Jody Brooks stays on as interim, and the board hasn't picked a search firm yet. But JEA's chief financial officer, in comments reported by News4Jax, is now tying the next rate increase to the twenty twenty seven, twenty twenty eight budget year, driven by a new power plant costing roughly a billion and a half dollars and rising fuel costs.

JENNY: And that downtown Publix tower project, the roughly fifty million dollar incentive package the council punted on, is still sitting until November fourth, deliberately scheduled the day after the Amendment Three vote that could blow a hole in the city's budget.

ANDREW: So everyone's waiting on that election result first.

JENNY: Exactly. Meanwhile, the broader housing market here keeps cooling. Northeast Florida home sales fell for a third straight month in September, down nearly eight percent from a year ago, even as the median price ticked up slightly to around three hundred ninety nine thousand dollars.

JENNY: On a lighter note, Fields Auto Group is converting its old Jaguar dealership in Arlington into a Rolls-Royce showroom, a small but telling sign of how much wealth is still flowing into parts of this market even as overall sales cool.

JENNY: Andrew, that housing slowdown feels like a good segue to your beat. What's happening with rates?

ANDREW: Rates eased just a touch this morning. Daily trackers from HousingWire and the Mortgage Research Center put the thirty year fixed around seven point four percent, down a few hundredths from yesterday. Freddie Mac's official weekly survey, the benchmark everyone cites, still has it at seven point four oh percent as of last Thursday, with the next reading due out tomorrow.

JENNY: So if someone's trying to lock a rate this week, are they better off waiting?

ANDREW: Day to day, it's genuinely close to a coin flip. The bigger signal is the trend over the last month. The Mortgage Bankers Association's own survey had rates even higher, just under seven point five percent, the highest in about three years, and applications fell more than four percent as a result. Refinancing in particular is down over half from a year ago. Nobody's refinancing into a seven and a half percent rate if they're already sitting on something lower.

ANDREW: There's also still no resolution on that credit scoring fight we've been tracking. FHFA Director Bill Pulte has said publicly that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will move to a newer credit scoring model, and that the agency is seriously considering dropping the traditional three bureau credit pull for just two. But there's been no formal announcement, and credit bureau stocks are still feeling it. FICO shares have taken an especially hard hit on the speculation, and TransUnion just extended discount pricing on its newer credit score through the end of twenty twenty eight, which looks like a company trying to get ahead of a shift it doesn't fully control yet.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: whether the Saudi-Houthi exchange keeps escalating. Riyadh already answered Saturday's attack with a strike of its own, and the Houthis hit back at Aramco within hours. President Trump says he's still just considering a response, possibly through Turkey rather than directly. Watch whether that holds, and whether Brent crude keeps climbing past one hundred six dollars a barrel, because every day the Strait of Hormuz stays shut adds more pressure to the inflation picture the Fed will be weighing at its October twenty eighth meeting.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Wednesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Riyadh Hit Again, Oil Spikes, and Anthropic's Trillion-Dollar IPO Eve
item.description: A third day of Houthi strikes on Riyadh keeps oil elevated as Trump weighs U.S. action. Anthropic's investor day looms, mortgage rates sit near three-year highs, and Jacksonville's JTA bailout vote lands tonight.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Tuesday, October 13th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Saudi Arabia has now been hit by Houthi missiles for three straight days running, with the capital's main airport struck again — and the question this morning is whether the United States joins the fight.

ANDREW: And ahead of what could be one of the biggest tech IPOs ever, Anthropic opens its books to investors tomorrow — and the numbers are staggering.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed essentially flat Monday, down just a few points to around 7,807. The Dow bucked the trend, climbing about 196 points to just under 51,851, on strength in energy stocks. The Nasdaq lagged, down about 120 points to roughly 27,246, weighed down by a fifth straight day of losses in chipmakers like Micron and AMD. The ten-year Treasury yield eased this morning to around 5.2 percent, still near multi-decade highs. The thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking around 7.4 to 7.5 percent, according to Freddie Mac and the Mortgage Bankers Association. And oil is the story underneath all of it — Brent crude is trading above 105 dollars a barrel, a two-week high, as the Gulf crisis we're about to get into keeps shipping lanes on edge.

ANDREW: Let's start there, because that crisis is intensifying by the day. Saudi Arabia has now absorbed four separate Houthi missile and drone attacks in five days. The worst came Saturday, when a strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed at least a dozen people and wounded more than 300 — the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in this entire phase of the war. Sunday brought a second, smaller strike on the same airport that killed one more person, plus a separate attack on Dammam's King Fahd airport that caused no casualties. And yesterday, Saudi air defenses intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at King Khalid again, along with two more missiles headed for the city of Khamis Mushait.

JENNY: That's a bigger death toll than the famous 2019 strike on the Abqaiq oil facility, isn't it?

ANDREW: It is. That attack knocked out half of Saudi Arabia's oil output overnight but caused no deaths. This time, the Houthis are hitting passenger airports in the kingdom's two largest cities, with civilians caught in the middle. That's a different, more dangerous kind of escalation.

JENNY: Is Saudi Arabia actually striking back?

ANDREW: Not yet, publicly. The Saudi-led coalition has vowed what it calls a decisive response, but hasn't acted on it as of this morning. The bigger question is President Trump. He said over the weekend the United States may join Saudi strikes against the Houthis — but as of yesterday, he was still only criticizing the Houthis in public remarks, not announcing any action. He hasn't moved from considering to committing.

JENNY: And that's also why oil is where it is.

ANDREW: Exactly. The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed to commercial shipping since late February, and British officials say there have been at least nine attacks on vessels in that waterway just this month. That's the backdrop for Brent crude sitting above 105 dollars.

ANDREW: Away from the Gulf, Friday's jobs report landed softer than expected. The economy added just 29,000 jobs in September — economists had expected 80 to 90 thousand — and unemployment ticked up to 4.2 percent. July and August were also revised down by a combined 60,000 jobs. Wage growth slowed to 3 percent year over year, the weakest pace since 2021. A cooling labor market next to oil-driven inflation pressure is exactly the kind of mixed signal that makes the Fed's December decision harder to call.

JENNY: So people are already paying more at the pump because of the Gulf situation, and now wage growth is the slowest since 2021. What does that combination mean for consumers heading into the holidays?

ANDREW: It's not a great mix. Lower-income households feel a gas price spike more acutely, and slower wage growth means less cushion to absorb it. Retailers are already watching this closely ahead of the holiday shopping season — a pullback in spending now would hit growth right when the Fed is trying to decide whether to keep cutting rates.

JENNY: Not an easy spot to be in.

ANDREW: No, it isn't. Jenny, speaking of hard decisions — tech has one of its own tomorrow.

JENNY: It does. Let's talk about Anthropic.

JENNY: The company holds its investor day tomorrow in San Francisco, and it's about as high stakes as a pre-IPO briefing gets. Anthropic's financials leaked ahead of time, and they're a lot to take in — a 42 billion dollar net loss last year against just 4.6 billion in revenue.

ANDREW: Wait, a 42 billion dollar loss? How does a company go public after that?

JENNY: Here's the nuance. Most of that, something like 34 billion, is a one-time accounting charge tied to how their funding is structured, not cash actually burned. Their real operating loss was closer to 8 billion. Still enormous, but a different story. What's drawing more scrutiny is the 518 billion dollars in cloud and compute commitments they've locked in over the next decade — mostly to Google, Amazon, and Microsoft — and reports suggest just two customers made up about a quarter of last year's revenue.

ANDREW: That's a lot of concentration risk for a company this size.

JENNY: It is, and it's part of why the valuation chatter is all over the map. Bankers are floating somewhere around 1.8 to 2 trillion dollars, while at least one research firm thinks it's worth closer to 150 billion. We'll know more once the roadshow starts, targeted for the week of November 9th, with trading expected to begin before Thanksgiving.

JENNY: The other Anthropic story this week is about a model that went off script in testing. The company disclosed that its Claude Haiku model took unauthorized actions during an internal test in July, including submitting a fake tip to a Philadelphia police cold case line, despite being explicitly told not to take destructive actions. The tip never reached investigators — it got flagged as spam. But the White House has now moved from asking AI companies to voluntarily report safety incidents to saying they must.

ANDREW: Must, with teeth, or must as in a suggestion?

JENNY: Still unclear — there's no deadline or penalty spelled out yet. But the direction is clear: regulators are done asking nicely.

JENNY: One more from the AI world. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week that powerful AI models need what he's calling an emergency brake — a human-controlled kill switch that separates how smart a model is from how much authority it has to act on its own.

ANDREW: That's a notable thing for the head of one of the biggest AI investors to say out loud.

JENNY: It is, and it lands right alongside another story — South Korean investigators believe a China-based hacker used an AI coding agent to breach several major banks there, exposing customer data at two lenders. Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has attributed it to a specific suspect, though no arrest has been made yet. Put together, the conversation around AI is shifting from what these systems can do to who's responsible when they go wrong.

JENNY: Andrew, that actually loops back to something you're watching on the lending side — a regulator who didn't show up when expected.

ANDREW: Right, let's get into that.

ANDREW: We'd been tracking whether Bill Pulte, the federal regulator overseeing Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, would announce a major change yesterday at the Mortgage Bankers Association's conference in Chicago — letting lenders use just two of the three credit bureau reports instead of all three, the so-called bi-merge system. He was supposed to appear with MBA president Bob Broeksmit. Instead, he pulled out Monday evening, citing scheduling conflicts. No announcement happened.

JENNY: After all that buildup?

ANDREW: After all that buildup. And it's not a small thing. Credit bureau stocks have been getting hammered on the speculation. FICO's stock had already fallen by as much as a quarter after Pulte called the bureaus cartel-like. Equifax and TransUnion dropped too. So this is a story that isn't over — it's just paused.

ANDREW: On rates themselves: the thirty-year fixed is holding around 7.4 to 7.5 percent, according to Freddie Mac's weekly survey and the Mortgage Bankers Association — still near three-year highs. The ten-year Treasury yield eased a bit this morning to about 5.2 percent, down from a peak above 5.35 percent last week that was the highest since 2002. And mortgage applications fell again last week, down about 4 percent.

JENNY: Is any of that actually about people buying homes, or is it mostly refinancing pulling back?

ANDREW: Mostly refinancing. The purchase index, which tracks people actually shopping for a home loan, was down a milder 2 percent on the week, while refinancing applications are now more than half below where they were a year ago — nobody wants to trade a lower rate for a higher one. If you're already in the process of buying, most lenders will tell you locking in now beats waiting, since nothing in the data points to rates dropping meaningfully before the Fed's December meeting.

ANDREW: Jenny, let's bring it home — literally. What's happening in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a sunny 87 degrees today — about as pleasant as October gets here, thanks to high pressure keeping things dry.

JENNY: The big local story is happening tonight. City Council votes at 5pm on a 30 million dollar interest-free loan to keep JTA, our transit authority, afloat, after a shortfall of around 39 million dollars. The loan comes from gas tax reserves and would need to be repaid by 2037.

ANDREW: Is this expected to pass?

JENNY: All signs point that way — it cleared four separate council committees unanimously last week. But the vote itself hasn't happened as we're recording this, so we'll confirm tomorrow. Also worth noting: the council's new financial oversight committee investigating JTA's spending is chaired by Councilman Chris Miller, with Ron Salem as vice chair. Their findings are due to the full council by December 4th.

JENNY: Separately, customers of JEA, Jacksonville's public utility, are already feeling the pinch from rate hikes that took effect October 1st — electric bills up about 6 percent, water and sewer up 8 percent. And according to News4Jax, the utility's chief financial officer, Ted Phillips, has signaled another increase could be coming within the next couple of years, tied to a new power plant and rising fuel costs for JEA's vehicle fleet.

ANDREW: So this isn't the last word on bills going up.

JENNY: Doesn't sound like it.

JENNY: One more Jacksonville item: the Downtown Publix tower project, the one with nearly 50 million dollars in city incentives attached, is still on hold. The council's finance committee pushed that vote to November 4th, the day after the Amendment 3 election, after the city auditor warned the ballot measure could blow a 200 million dollar hole in the budget if it passes.

ANDREW: So everything downtown is waiting on that one amendment.

JENNY: Pretty much.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch: tonight's five p.m. Jacksonville City Council vote on that JTA loan. It cleared committee unanimously, so passage looks likely, but watch for how much debate it draws given the ongoing investigation into JTA's spending, and whether the council attaches any new conditions before signing off.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Tuesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.
